content:
Good night-time lighting is one of the simplest ways to make the trip from bed to the toilet safer when arthritis makes you stiff and slow first thing. Have a light you can switch on before you put your feet on the floor, plug-in or motion-sensor lights along the route, and a light in the bathroom you can find without fumbling. Sit on the edge of the bed for a moment before standing, wear proper footwear, use your walking aid and keep the route clear. If you are getting up several times a night, or have fallen or nearly fallen at night, tell your GP: there may be a medicine, bladder or blood pressure cause that can be treated.

This guide is about lighting and the route at night. If the main problem is needing the toilet often, see night-time toilet trips; if a bedside commode might help, see commodes at night. If you have already had a fall, start with rebuilding confidence after a fall.

Why night-time is a risky time to move

Several things stack up at night. Joints are often at their stiffest after lying still, so the first few steps are slow and short. Eyes take time to adjust from dark to light, and older eyes need more light to see edges, steps and rugs. Blood pressure can dip when you stand up quickly, which can make you light-headed. You may be half-asleep, in a hurry to reach the toilet, and wearing loose slippers or socks. Some medicines, such as sleeping tablets and some painkillers, make this worse. Good lighting will not fix all of that, but it removes one of the easiest problems to solve.

Light the whole route, not just the room

  • Before your feet touch the floor: a bedside lamp with a large, easy switch, a touch lamp, or a light you can turn on with a remote or voice speaker. Avoid lamps you have to grip a small knob to switch on if your hands are sore
  • Along the way: plug-in night lights or battery motion-sensor lights at floor or skirting-board level on the route from bed to bathroom, including the landing and the top and bottom of any stairs
  • In the bathroom: a light that comes on easily, such as a motion-sensor light or a long pull cord you can reach without stretching
  • Warm, soft light is fine: it should be bright enough to see the floor, edges and steps, but not so harsh that it dazzles you or wakes you fully
  • Stairs: light both ends, and switches at the top and the bottom if you can. Never use the stairs in the dark

Plug-in and stick-on motion-sensor lights are widely available and usually inexpensive. If you are not sure what would work in your home, an occupational therapist or a council home assessment can advise (see below).

Getting up safely in the night

  1. Switch the light on first, then wait a moment for your eyes to adjust
  2. Sit up and stay sitting on the edge of the bed for a minute. Gently move your ankles and knees to wake up stiff joints
  3. Stand up slowly, holding something steady. If you feel dizzy or light-headed, sit back down until it passes
  4. Put on proper footwear — well-fitting slippers with a back and a grip sole, not socks or backless mules
  5. Use your stick or frame at night if you use one by day, and keep it within reach of the bed
  6. Take your time. Rushing to the toilet is a common reason for night-time falls

Our sit-to-stand practice guide helps with getting up from the bed and toilet with less effort.

Clear the route

  • Remove or secure loose rugs, trailing cables and clutter on the route between bed and bathroom
  • Keep the bedroom door and bathroom door open, or easy to push, so you are not fiddling with handles in the dark
  • Put a chair or something steady to hold along a long route, and ask about grab rails beside the toilet and on the stairs
  • Keep glasses, your phone or alarm, and a glass of water within reach of the bed

When it is more than lighting

Talk to your GP or pharmacist if any of these apply:

  • You are getting up to pee more often than you used to, or it is disturbing your sleep. Needing to go more at night often comes with age, but NHS guidance notes it can have treatable causes, including some medicines such as water tablets, drinking late in the evening, an overactive bladder, a urine infection and prostate problems
  • You feel dizzy or light-headed when you stand up. Some blood pressure tablets and other medicines can cause this. See blood pressure tablets and falls
  • You take sleeping tablets, strong painkillers or other medicines that make you drowsy. See sleeping tablets and falls, and ask for a medication review. Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself — ask first
  • Your eyesight has changed. Have a regular eye test; see eyesight and falls
  • Night pain is stopping you sleeping. See restless nights with joint pain
  • You have had a fall or a near miss. NICE recommends that people who have fallen are asked about it and offered a falls assessment where appropriate, which can include a home hazard check

Help with your home

You can ask your local council for a free care needs assessment. This can lead to an occupational therapy visit and small equipment or adaptations such as grab rails. Some areas also have handyperson services that fit rails and lights. Age UK can tell you what is available locally.

If you live alone

Keep a phone or a personal alarm within reach at night, including in the bathroom. Make a plan for what you would do if you fell and could not get up; see a falls plan if you live alone.

If you fall at night

Stay calm and check whether you are hurt before trying to move. If you are not hurt and feel able to, the NHS advises rolling onto your hands and knees, crawling to a sturdy chair, and getting up slowly. If you are hurt or cannot get up, call for help and keep warm while you wait. Call 999 if you have hurt your head, cannot move, are bleeding heavily or think you have broken a bone. For urgent advice that is not an emergency, contact NHS 111. Tell your GP about any fall, even if you were not hurt.

For carers

  • Walk the route at night yourself with the lights on and off, and look for dark patches, steps and trip hazards
  • Check bulbs and night-light batteries regularly
  • Notice new night-time confusion. A sudden change can be a sign of infection; see urinary infections and sudden confusion

Common questions

Will a night light keep me awake?

A dim, warm light at floor level is usually fine for sleep. Motion-sensor lights that only come on when you get up avoid the problem altogether.

Is a commode better than walking to the toilet?

For some people, at some times, yes — for example during a bad flare or after an illness. It is a personal choice; an occupational therapist can help you decide. See commodes at night.
